adversarial_critique: Claude's numerical extraction and directional coding are fully supported by the primary empirical analysis: in Table 3 (PDF p. 15, N = 593), non-notified households consumed 37.3% fewer litres per capita per day (LPCD) than notified reference households after adjusting for household size, per capita income, and religion (95% CI: –46.4% to –26.5%, p < 0.001; unadjusted –38.2%), with 38.7% of the total association mediated by water infrastructure, accessibility, reliability, and cost in GSEM path analysis (PDF p. 12; Figure 3, p. 16). Every water-specific robustness check and bivariate indicator reinforces this finding, including 3.4 higher adjusted odds of severe water deprivation (⩽20 LPCD) in multivariate logistic regression (PDF p. 12) and worse in-home tap access (2.6% vs. 9.9%), higher median unit water price (407 vs. 219 INR/1000L), and higher income share spent on water (11% vs. 9%, p = 0.01) in Table 2 (PDF pp. 11, 13–14). Restating the exposure orientation from the paper's regression contrast (non-notified vs. notified, raw sign –) to Family A's canonical legal-recognition pole (notified vs. non-notified = Favourable) is substantively valid, though retaining 'Non-notified slum status' in `exposure_short` creates a column-display hazard if read without `exposure_orientation` and `coding_note`. Adversarially, `exposure_full` slightly overstates the role of the 2014 *Pani Haq Samiti* Bombay High Court order because the 2016 survey was explicitly fielded *before* that order was implemented (PDF p. 5), and legal status was operationalized ecologically by neighbourhood (Matangrushi Nagar vs. Indira Nagar) rather than verified via individual pre-2000 household documents (PDF pp. 4, 17). Minor secondary nuances—a mixed unadjusted sanitation distribution in Table 1 (higher open defecation [4.5% vs. 2.1%] alongside higher home toilets [12.6% vs. 6.0%] in the non-notified neighbourhood, p = 0.005, PDF p. 10) and a null difference in child school absence from water collection (p = 0.18, Table 2, PDF p. 14)—do not affect the primary water-access verdict, and the dossier's provenance string merely confuses issue pagination (pp. 181–190) and section `II.c` with the 21-page OnlineFirst PDF (PDF pp. 4, 12, 15; section `I.c`).

numerical_check_note: All stored numerical values match the source PDF exactly: adjusted multivariate % difference = –37.3% (95% CI: –46.4%, –26.5%; p < 0.001) and univariate % difference = –38.2% (<0.001) in Table 3 (PDF p. 15); GSEM mediation share = 38.7% (unmediated –38.2%, residual direct –23.4%, PDF p. 12 & Figure 3, p. 16); and N = 593 households (283 notified, 310 non-notified; 7 of 600 sampled households excluded for missing water data, PDF pp. 8–10). Minor provenance discrepancies in the dossier: the AI location note cites final journal issue pages (p. 181–182, p. 189–190) rather than the 21-page OnlineFirst PDF pagination (PDF pp. 4, 12, 15) and cites Section II.c (which is 'Data collection' on PDF p. 7) instead of Section I.c ('The legal backdrop...', PDF p. 4); the automated PDF author-match warning is a false alarm (`Maya Lubeck-Schricker` is printed on PDF p. 1).
polarity_or_orientation_issue: No coding error, but an important orientation restatement and label mismatch to watch: Table 3 models `Non-notified` against `Notified (Ref)` on log-LPCD (`higher = better`), giving `raw_coefficient_sign = "-"`. Claude explicitly sets `exposure_orientation = "restated to the recognised pole"` so `substantive_direction = "Favourable"` correctly represents the benefit of legal notification/recognition. However, `exposure_short` ('Non-notified slum status') and `comparator_short` ('notified slums') still state the unreversed exclusion contrast, so any summary table displaying `exposure_short` beside `Favourable` without `exposure_orientation` could be misread as saying non-notified status is favourable (mathematically, reversing the reference group to non-notified yields +59.5% higher LPCD for notified households).
